methods: Exact COL26.8 queue rows and all indexed dossier shards checked for existing dossier and source stable-ID duplicates.
Repository text and source files searched for each COL ID, scientific name, article title, and DOI.
Public GitHub issues and pull requests searched across all states for each COL ID, scientific name, and DOI.
duplicateAudit.limitations: This audit covers the selected repository and public issue/PR search results at the checked time; it is not a claim that no related research exists.

species.scope: The source supports a controlled microfiber-exposure observation in adult laboratory-colony Japanese medaka; it does not establish a wild-population effect, environmental threshold, or species-wide response.

lifeStatusScope.wild: Wild-population responses were not assessed; the study used a laboratory colony.
lifeStatusScope.domesticated: The article describes laboratory-colony adults and does not establish domestication status or assess domesticated populations.
lifeStatusScope.fossil: Fossil occurrence and geological age have not been assessed.

sources.title: Hu et al. (2020), Chronic microfiber exposure in adult Japanese medaka (Oryzias latipes)
sources.version: PLOS ONE 15(3): e0229962; version of record published 2020-03-09
sources.locator: Methods §§2.3–2.6; Results §3.4 and Fig. 4; item-level copyright and license notice.
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), linked from the publisher article copyright notice.
sources.scope: Original laboratory study of adult Oryzias latipes exposed to polyester or polypropylene microfibers; claims are limited to the reported colony, exposure concentration and duration, and histology sample.
sources.rightsHolder: Hu et al., as identified by the PLOS ONE article.
sources.licenseEvidenceLocator: The article-level copyright notice links the Creative Commons Attribution License to the canonical CC BY 4.0 URL.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: Published article text; this dossier paraphrases findings and does not reproduce figures or separately credited third-party material.
sources.attribution: Hu L, Chernick M, Lewis AM, Ferguson PL, Hinton DE (2020). Chronic microfiber exposure in adult Japanese medaka (Oryzias latipes). PLOS ONE 15(3):e0229962. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0229962. Findings paraphrased.

claims.text: In this controlled exposure experiment, fusion of secondary gill lamellae was reported in 33% of adult medaka exposed to polyester microfibers and 67% exposed to polypropylene microfibers at 10,000 fibers/L for 21 days; no fusion was observed in controls. Histology used six fish per treatment. The authors also noted minor petechiae and epithelial lifting in some control gills.
claims.locator: Methods §§2.3–2.6; Results §3.4 and Fig. 4, including the control comparison and histology sample description.
claims.placeTimeScope: Adults from a laboratory colony were exposed in a dedicated room at 24°C under a 14:10 light:dark cycle for 21 days. The article does not report calendar dates or a wild collection locality for the experimental fish.
claims.lifeStatus: Captive laboratory-colony adults; no wild fish or fossil material was assessed.

gaps: The histology sample was six fish per treatment from one laboratory colony, and the reported concentration is not an environmental threshold.
The study does not establish responses in wild populations, across strains, or at lower environmental exposure levels.
Morphology outside this exposure response, life history, other ecology, evolution, distribution, fossils, conservation, and independent review remain unassessed.

completenessReasons: One controlled microfiber experiment supports only the reported adult laboratory-colony histology outcome.
The colony, exposure level, duration, and small histology sample do not establish broader population responses or environmental thresholds.
Most biological facets and complete geographic, fossil, conservation, and external review coverage remain unassessed.

species.scope: The source compares transcript profiles from the reported artificially cultured mycelium and mature fruiting-body samples. Culture stage and medium differ together, so the results do not isolate a causal stage effect or represent all strains or wild populations.

lifeStatusScope.wild: No wild field material is reported for the transcriptome comparison; the source does not establish the culture strain's wild origin.
lifeStatusScope.domesticated: Artificially cultivated mycelium and fruiting-body material were studied; domesticated population-level variation was not assessed.
lifeStatusScope.fossil: Fossil occurrence and geological age have not been assessed.

sources.title: Yin et al. (2012), Genome-Wide Transcriptome and Proteome Analysis on Different Developmental Stages of Cordyceps militaris
sources.version: PLOS ONE 7(12):e51853; version of record published 2012-12-14
sources.locator: Abstract; Introduction study overview; Methods, Sample Preparation and differential-expression threshold; publisher copyright notice and DOI-deposited Crossref license metadata.
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0); the article states Creative Commons Attribution and the DOI-deposited Crossref license metadata specifies the CC BY 4.0 URL.
sources.scope: Original transcriptome and proteome comparison of two artificially cultivated C. militaris sample types; claims are limited to those samples and the study's differential-expression analysis.
sources.rightsHolder: Yin et al., as identified by the PLOS ONE article.
sources.licenseEvidenceLocator: The article copyright notice states Creative Commons Attribution; DOI-deposited Crossref license metadata gives the CC BY 4.0 URL. The metadata's content-version field is unspecified, so no more specific version label is inferred.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: Published article text; this dossier paraphrases findings and does not reproduce figures, tables, or separately credited third-party material.
sources.attribution: Yin Y, Yu G, Chen Y, Jiang S, Wang M, Jin Y, et al. (2012). Genome-Wide Transcriptome and Proteome Analysis on Different Developmental Stages of Cordyceps militaris. PLOS ONE 7(12):e51853. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0051853. Findings paraphrased.

claims.text: A transcriptome comparison of the study's artificially cultivated Cordyceps militaris mycelium and mature fruiting-body samples identified 2,712 differentially expressed genes: 2,113 were reported as up-regulated in mycelium and 599 in fruiting body under the stated thresholds. This describes the two analyzed samples, not a species-wide developmental rule.
claims.locator: Abstract and study overview; Methods, Differential Expression Analysis (FDR ≤ 0.001 and |log2 RPKM ratio| ≥ 1).
claims.placeTimeScope: Artificial cultures were incubated at 22°C: mycelium on PDA for 18 days in darkness; fruiting-body material was grown on rice medium through dark and 16:8-hour light:dark phases. The article reports sequencing at BGI in Shenzhen, China, but not the cultivation site or calendar dates.
claims.lifeStatus: Artificially cultivated mycelium and mature fruiting-body samples; the source does not identify the strain's wild provenance or assess natural populations.

gaps: Mycelium and fruiting-body samples were grown on different media, confounding developmental material with culture conditions.
The transcriptome comparison reports two sample types without biological replication, so it does not establish strain-wide or species-wide expression patterns.
Morphology, other life-history traits, ecology, evolution, distribution, fossils, conservation, and independent review remain unassessed.

completenessReasons: The developmental transcriptome result comes from two artificially cultivated sample types on different media, so stage and medium are confounded.
The study does not establish population-level variation or general developmental patterns across strains or natural populations.
Most biological facets and complete geographic, fossil, conservation, and external review coverage remain unassessed.

species.scope: The source supports a captive-enclosure temperature comparison in one Brock University study. It does not show that the enclosure design improves wild adaptation, thermoregulation, or overall welfare.

lifeStatusScope.wild: The temperature comparison used captive-bred animals and laboratory enclosures; wild population responses were not assessed.
lifeStatusScope.domesticated: Captive-bred lizards from two breeders were studied; domesticated population-level variation was not assessed.
lifeStatusScope.fossil: Fossil occurrence and geological age have not been assessed.

sources.title: Denommé et al. (2025), Influence of enclosure design on the behaviour and welfare of Pogona vitticeps
sources.version: PLOS ONE 20(6):e0322682; version of record published 2025-06-05
sources.locator: Methods, Animals and husbandry and Thermal heterogeneity; Results, Thermal heterogeneity and enclosure temperatures; publisher copyright and license notice.
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), linked from the publisher article copyright notice.
sources.scope: Original study of captive-bred Pogona vitticeps in standard and naturalistic enclosure conditions; the cited thermal comparison is limited to the measured enclosures and time points.
sources.rightsHolder: Denommé et al., as identified by the PLOS ONE article.
sources.licenseEvidenceLocator: The article-level copyright notice links the Creative Commons Attribution License to the canonical CC BY 4.0 URL.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: Published article text; this dossier paraphrases findings and does not reproduce figures or separately credited third-party material.
sources.attribution: Denommé M, Bakker NL, Tattersall GJ (2025). Influence of enclosure design on the behaviour and welfare of Pogona vitticeps. PLOS ONE 20(6):e0322682. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0322682. Findings paraphrased.

claims.text: Thermal images from the study's naturalistic enclosures showed greater substrate-temperature variability than standard enclosures: model estimates for the substrate-temperature standard deviation were 1.86 ± 0.07 and 1.39 ± 0.07, respectively (p < 0.001). The result is an enclosure-level measurement and does not by itself demonstrate improved thermoregulation or welfare.
claims.locator: Results, Thermal heterogeneity and enclosure temperatures; Methods, Thermal heterogeneity; Fig. 8.
claims.placeTimeScope: Brock University laboratory study in St. Catharines, Ontario, Canada. Temperature images were collected in May 2024 around 09:00, 11:00, and 15:00; after removing one enclosure of each style from analysis, 11 enclosures per style were represented at each time point.
claims.lifeStatus: Captive-bred Pogona vitticeps in laboratory enclosures; no wild animals or fossil material were represented in this temperature comparison.

gaps: The temperature analysis measured enclosures and did not establish the lizards' resulting body temperatures or realized thermoregulation.
The authors describe overall behaviour and welfare effects as equivocal; substrate-temperature heterogeneity alone does not establish improved welfare.
Morphology, life history, wild ecology, evolution, distribution, fossils, conservation, and independent review remain unassessed.

completenessReasons: The enclosure study supports a thermal heterogeneity result but does not establish corresponding thermoregulation or welfare effects.
The evidence is limited to captive-bred animals in one laboratory study and does not represent wild populations.
Most biological facets and complete geographic, fossil, conservation, and external review coverage remain unassessed.
